# Development and validation of an artificial intelligence literacy assessment for kindergarten children

**Jiahong Su**[^1]

Received: 10 May 2023 / Accepted: 1 August 2023 © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2024

**Abstract** With Artificial intelligence (AI) literacy gaining more and more attention at the kindergarten level, it is becoming critical to assess the AI literacy levels of kinder- garten children and develop appropriate courses to enhance their foundational AI knowledge and skills. This study proposes and validates a comprehensive AI lit- eracy assessment tool (AI4KGA) for kindergarten children. The research involved 215 children and 19 experts. The validity and reliability of the AI4KG assessment were evaluated by experts, with Cronbach’s _α_ and Item Response Theory approach. The results demonstrated that the AI literacy assessment (AI4KGA) was valid and reliable. We also found that younger children scored lower on the AI literacy assess- ment than older children and girls demonstrated a slightly higher AI literacy score than boys after they completed the AI4KG curriculum. The AI4KGA has potential applications for various stakeholders, such as policymakers, educators, instructional designers, researchers, and educational institutions. The findings suggest that the AI4KGA can evaluate children’s learning outcomes in terms of AI literacy. Over- all, this research contributes to developing AI literacy assessment in kindergarten children and advancing AI literacy education.

**Keywords** AI literacy · AI literacy assessment · AI4KGA · AI literacy education · Validation · Early childhood education · Kindergarten children

 Jiahong Su maggiesu@connect.hku.hk

**1 Introduction**

AI has become increasingly vital in the modern world. Artificial intelligence (AI) has widely applicable in various domains, such as healthcare (Jiang et al., [2017)](#declarations) and education (Su & Yang, 2022). Therefore, it is essential to introduce AI concepts or knowledge to students at an early age (Su et al., 2023b). Incorporating AI into the educational curriculum has become a crucial issue in K–12 education, as highlighted by recent studies (e.g., Yue et al., 2022; Su et al., 2022, 2023a). AI literacy is “the ability to express ourselves and communicate using written language” (Long & Mag- erko, 2020, p.2).

Some scholars have designed AI literacy assessment for adults (Wang et al., 2022) or older students (Kong et al., 2023; Ng et al., 2023). Specifically, Wang et al. (2022) developed a 12-item scale for assessing adult users’ AI literacy, which includes four dimensions: awareness, usage, evaluation, and ethics. Laupichler et al. (2023) developed a 38-item scale for assessing non-experts’ AI literacy. Kong et al. (2023a) employed concept tests and self-reflective writing to evaluate the AI literacy of senior secondary students. However, none of these measures have been applied to kindergarten students, probably because the tested concepts are beyond the cognitive development level of kindergarten children (Su et al., 2023b). It is crucial to note that, considering their limited literacy comprehension abilities, the development of an assessment which does not require literacy comprehension is necessary for mea- suring children’s AI literacy.

Considering the lack of existing AI literacy assessment tools for kindergarten chil- dren (Su et al., 2023b), this study aims to develop and validate an AI literacy assess- ment specifically designed for this age group. This study aims to fill a significant research gap by offering valuable insights into the development of AI literacy assess- ments among kindergarten children. The assessment will be specifically designed to ensure its ease of administration, comprehension, and scoring for kindergarten chil- dren, thereby serving as a crucial tool for educators and researchers to evaluate the effectiveness of AI literacy education programs tailored to kindergarten children. The aim of this study is to develop valid and reliable measures for kindergarten children’s AI literacy.

**2 Literature review**

**2.1 AI literacy**

The term ‘AI literacy’ was initially introduced by Burgsteiner et al. ([2016)](#declarations) and Kan- dlhofer et al. (2016). _AI literacy_ refers to the competencies necessary for understand- ing the basic knowledge and concepts associated with AI (Kandlhofer et al., 2016). According to other scholars, _AI literacy_ was defined as “having the essential abili- ties that people need to live, learn and work in our digital world through AI-driven technologies, and this should be taught at the K-12 levels” (Ng et al., 2021, p. 2). Long and Magerko (2020) expanded the definition of ‘AI literacy to encompass a broader range of competencies. These competencies empower individuals to effec-

tively assess, communicate, and collaborate with AI, enabling them to utilize AI in diverse settings, including online environments, at home, and in the workplace. Recently, several studies developed an AI literacy framework in education (e.g., Kong et al., 2023b; Ng et al., 2021; Wong et al., 2020). Ng et al. (2021) developed an AI literacy framework that includes four dimensions: (1) know & understand AI; (2) use & apply AI; (3) evaluate & create AI; and (4) AI ethics. These dimensions offer a comprehensive framework that supports the development of AI literacy and enables the integration of AI into early childhood education (Su et al., 2023a).

**2.2 AI literacy in early childhood education**

AI literacy indicated in ECE mentioned in the studies by Su and Zhong (2022) and Su et al. (2023b): (1) the significance of introducing AI education to kindergarten children; (2) whether kindergarten children could understand basic AI knowledge or concepts; and (3) which teaching method is suitable for teaching AI to kindergarten- ers (Su et al., 2023b).

There are several reasons why kindergarten children should be engaged in AI learning. To begin, knowing and understanding the basic concepts of AI and using AI applications are vital for all members of society to effectively live, learn, and work in today’s digital world (Ng et al., 2021). For example, many artificial intelligence applications are used in daily life, such as Siri and facial recognition. Therefore, early exposure to these technologies will help children better understand and apply them. Second, some studies found that learning AI can enhance various skills, such as creativity (Su & Yang, 2023b) and inquiry skills (Kewalramani et al., 2021). For example, Su and Yang (2023a) found that learning AI could enhance kindergarten children’s creativity skills. Lastly, all children need to have access to AI education, particularly as AI toys become more accessible in today’s society (Kewalramani et al., 2021). Early AI education can significantly bridge the digital divide and ensure equal opportunities for children from diverse backgrounds.

Su and Zhong (2022) proposed an AI literacy framework for kindergarten children, including AI knowledge, AI skills, and AI attitudes. Afterward, Su and Yang (2023b) revised this AI knowledge of AI literacy framework includes powerful ideas of AI 

1. AI is trained by humans (2) humans use big data to train AI, (3) AI is trained to solve problems and to help humans, and (4) AI has its limitations, machine learning, and potential ethical issues of using AI technologies. These dimensions align with AI4K12.org’s AI literacy for K-12 students. The ideas presented in these dimensions also encompass more advanced concepts, such as machine learning and the ethi- cal considerations associated with AI technology (Su & Zhong, 2022). Su and Yang (2023a) redeveloped the Five big ideas of AI for young children, namely perceptions, representation and reasoning, learning, natural interaction, and societal impact. This framework aims to equip researchers and educators with strategies for successfully integrating introductory AI education into early childhood classrooms. Several studies found that kindergarten children can understand basic AI concepts and knowledge (e.g., Williams et al., 2019a; Su & Yang, 2023b). Williams et al. (2019a) developed an AI curriculum for kindergarten children to enhance their under- standing of AI concepts. Results showed that kindergarten children can understand 

three basic AI concepts: knowledge-based systems, supervised machine learning, and generative AI. Su and Yang (2023a) designed an AI literacy curriculum based on Su and Zhong (2022)’s framework. Findings showed that kindergarten children can know basic AI concepts and knowledge. Therefore, we believe that kindergar- ten children can understand basic AI concepts and knowledge through appropriate curriculum.

Different scholars employ different teaching methods to introduce AI literacy to kindergarten children. These teaching methods include customized platforms, play- based learning, project-based learning, and a story approach to integrated learning (SAIL). Two studies adopted customized platforms to teach AI knowledge to kinder- garteners (e.g., Lin et al., 2020; Williams et al., 2019a). Research has discovered that kindergarten children can explore and comprehend AI’s fundamentals and key con- cepts through AI robots or conversational platforms like PopBots and Zhorai (e.g., Lin et al., 2020; Williams et al., 2019a). These AI robots and conversational platforms provide age-appropriate learning experiences that enable children to engage with AI in an accessible and enjoyable manner. The other three teaching methods used in teaching AI were play-based learning, project-based learning, and story approach to integrated learning (SAIL) (Su & Yang, 2023a).

AI literacy in primary and secondary is also very important (Su et al., 2023b). AI literacy is crucial in the 21st century. By learning about AI, students become familiar with fundamental concepts and enhanced their technical and communication skills (Su et al., 2023a). For example, Chiu et al. ([2021)](#declarations) used pre- and post-questionnaires to evaluate students’ AI knowledge (e.g., the basis of AI knowledge, AI reasoning, AI and ethics, and AI and the future of work). After learning the AI course, post- questionnaire results show that students gained more AI knowledge in such aspects as fundamentals of AI, AI reasoning, societal good, social impact and challenges of AI, AI and Ethics, and AI and future of work. Some researchers found that learning AI can enhance several skills, such as technical skills (Chiu et al., [2021)](#declarations) and com- munication skills (Ng, 2021). For example, Ng (2021) indicated that extracurricular activities (i.e., teaching AI through a social networking site) in AI courses can help students develop their social skills (e.g., communication skills).

**2.3 AI literacy assessment**

Using validated measurement instruments is necessary and valuable in any research area (Román-González et al., 2017). Most research on AI literacy assessment has focused on older students, adolescents, or adults (e.g., Chai et al., [2021;](#declarations) Wang et al., 2022; Kong et al., 2023a, b). For example, Chai et al. ([2021)](#declarations) developed a survey questionnaire to assess primary school students’ behavioural intentions to learn AI, including five dimensions: self-efficacy in learning AI, AI readiness, perceived use of AI for social good, AI literacy, and behavioural intention. Wang et al. (2022) devel- oped a 12-item scale to measure AI literacy among adult users of AI technology. In addition, Pinski and Benlian (2023) developed a general AI literacy scale for adults. Kong et al. (2023a) used concept tests and reflective writing to measure senior sec- ondary students’ AI literacy. Laupichler et al. (2023) developed an AI literacy test to assess non-experts’ AI literacy. Ng et al. (2022) used a knowledge test to assess pri-

mary school students’ AI literacy. Ng et al. (2023) developed an AI literacy question- naire to assess secondary schools students’ literacy development. However, none of these measurement instruments are appropriate for assessing kindergarten children. Although extensive research has exists on AI literacy in older children, adoles- cents, and adults, further research is needed for kindergarten children to develop and assess their AI literacy. The current measurement methods for AI literacy, such as the tools developed by Chai et al. ([2021)](#declarations), Wang et al. (2022), Pinski and Benlian (2023), Kong et al. (2023a), Laupichler et al. (2023), and Ng et al. (2022, 2023) are not suit- able for kindergarten children due to their complexity and focus on adult users of AI technology or primary and secondary school students’ AI literacy. Therefore, there is a need to develop an AI literacy assessment for kindergarten children. A developmental approach can be adopted when designing standards for assess- ing AI literacy in kindergarten children. This may involve identifying the key concepts and skills children need to understand and developto be AI literate. For example, the “Powerful Ideas” about AI proposed by Su and Yang (2023a) can serve as the foundation for assessing the development of AI literacy in kindergarten children.

In addition to developing such standards for assessing AI literacy, it is also help- ful to determine whether the development of AI literacy is age-related. Some studies have found developmental differences in children’s understanding and learning of AI. For example, Su et al. (2023a) found that AI literacy differs significantly across vari- ous age groups, including kindergarten (3–5 years old), primary (6–12 years old), and secondary (13–18 years old). Kindergarten children (3–5 years old) only understand basic AI concepts and knowledge. However, primary (6–12 years old) and secondary (13–18 years old) school students can comprehend complex AI concepts (Su et al., 2023a). Therefore, further research is needed to explore whether age-related differ- ences exist in developing AI literacy in kindergarten children.

**Research Questions** Given the gaps in the existing literature and the significance of developing valid and reliable measures for assessing AI literacy among kindergar- ten children, we propose the two research questions (RQs).

**2.3.1 RQ1: Is the AI4KGA a valid and reliable measure of kindergarten children’s AI literacy?**

To address this question, a new AI literacy assessment for kindergarten children, namely AI4KGA, was developed based on the powerful ideas of AI identified by Su and Yang (2023b), AI curriculum’s framework for kindergarten children (Su & Zhong, 2022), and the AI literacy dimensions proposed by Ng et al. (2021). The design of this assessment considered the cognitive abilities and developmental needs of kindergarten children.

**2.3.2 RQ2: How does kindergarten children’s AI literacy relate to their age and gender?**

The second research questions investigate the correlation between children’s age and gender and their development of AI literacy. By administering the AI4KGA to a diverse sample of kindergarten children, we conducted data analysis to ascer- tain if there exists a significant association between age, gender, and AI literacy. The outcomes of this research aim to provide valuable insights to educators and policymakers, aiding in their comprehension of the developmental progression of AI literacy during early childhood. Additionally, these findings can contribute to designing AI literacy curricula and learning experiences suitable for different age groups.

**3 Methods**

The objective of this study was to develop valid and reliable measures for kindergar- ten children’s AI literacy. The research study employed a mixed-methods research design (Leech et al., 2010), integrating qualitative and quantitative approaches. The data were collected through AI literacy assessment, open-ended questions in surveys, and individual interviews. This methodology is in line with the previous study on developing computational thinking (CT) assessment for K-12 students and higher education (Weese, 2016).

**3.1 Participants**

This study involved 215 children aged between 3 and 6 years (M = 5.02, SD = 0.76) who were enrolled in eight classes at several kindergartens located in Hong Kong, China. There were 121 boys and 94 girls, as indicated in Table 1. The final sample consisted of 215 children because all children participated in the post-test. We admin- istered an assessment after the eight-week course of AI literacy education because no parent had reported that their child had previously studied AI. In addition, 19 experts were involved in the evaluation of the AI literacy assessment to determine its con- struct, content, and face validity.

**3.2 Course design and procedures**

The AI4KG curriculum was delivered in eight 35-minute sessions in several Hong Kong kindergartens. The AI4KG program for the AI classes is a curriculum designed according to the powerful ideas of AI (Su & Yang, 2023b) and AI learning tools.

**3.3 Data collection and analysis**

The _AI4KG children’s AI literacy assessment_ (AI4KGA) was developed based on a search of the vast literature which focused on kindergarten children’s AI literacy (e.g., Su et al., 2023a; Williams et al., 2019a). Prior to conducting this AI4KGA, the research team provided training to the two research assistants (RAs). Subsequently, the first author and RAs read the assessment questions aloud to the kindergarten student to minimize the effects of literacy level on the outcome of the AI4KGA. All the 16 items were in a multiple-choice format, with a score of 1 point given for each correct answer and a score of 0 points for each incorrect answer.

- **Aim**: AI4KGA aims to assess the development level of AI literacy of kindergar- ten children.
- **Target population**: AI4KGA is mainly designed and intended for kindergarten children between 3 and 6 years old.
- **Instrument Type**: multiple choice test (only one correct).
- **Length and estimated completion time**: 16 items; 25 min.

Moreover, the parents were requested to furnish fundamental details about their chil- dren such as their names, ages, and gender. Prior to administering the AI4KGA to kindergarten children, a group of experts meticulously scrutinized the assessment to verify the precision and usefulness of each statement. In line with El-Hamamsy et al.’s ([2022)](#declarations) research, we employed the expert assessment technique to evaluate the AI4KGA’s face, construct, and content validity.

Many researchers have utilized _expert evaluations_ as an approach to validate assessments in educational research (e.g., Adams & Wieman, [2011;](#declarations) Walker & Fraser, 2005). Therefore, before administering the AI4KGA to kindergarten children, a panel of experts was assembled to assess if AI literacy questions are a way to measure kin- dergarten children’s understanding of basic AI knowledge (construct validity), deter- mine if the assessment is clear illustrations to explain questions and options (face validity), and evaluate whether the assessment is appropriate for kindergarten chil- dren (content validity). A total of 19 experts with diverse backgrounds participated in the evaluation of the AI literacy assessment for kindergarten children (refer to Table 2). The experts were recruited from:

1. Researchers in education field dedicated to fostering and/or evaluating AI lit- eracy issues.
2. Education professionals involved in local/mainland/international education to gain a better understand the suitability of the suitability of AI development. This included (a) AI researchers from the faculty of education in universities and (b) teachers who have received AI education training and are currently teaching AI concepts and knowledge to their target age group.

The expert evaluation was divided into two components. Initially, the experts were requested to complete the survey provided in Table 3, which was adapted from El- Hamamsy et al.’s ([2022)](#declarations) research. The survey consisted of two main parts: the first part collected demographic information, while the second part evaluated the AI4KG assess- ment and comprised three main components: the evaluation of individual questions, the evaluation of individual blocks, and an overall assessment of the AI4KGA evalu- ation. Furthermore, the experts were asked to provide feedback and suggestions for improving each question of the AI4KG assessment. Subsequently, five selected experts were individually interviewed to discuss their impressions of the AI4KG assessment and provide recommendations for improvement. The research areas of these experts selected by the researchers are educational technology, including AI in education (AIED) and AI literacy. They are experienced researchers in the field of education.

**3.3.1 Ethics**

In this research, we adhered to the ethical guidelines established by the university’s internal committee. Before conducting the study, informed consent was obtained from the teachers, the parents/caregivers of the children, and the children, who pro- vided their oral consent. The participants voluntarily participate in the research, and no participant’s identity was revealed.

**3.4 Data analysis**

Regarding the qualitative methods, audio recordings of all the expert interviews were made to facilitate transcription and analysis at a later stage of the study. To create thematic networks, the transcripts, codes, and analyses of both the survey and inter- views were utilized, following the methodology proposed by Attride-stirling ([2001)](#declarations). The data was categorized and coded according to several main themes. To minimize researcher subjectivity, the data analysis approach involved the first author and two research assistants working separately. The author first identified all the codes related to content validity and recommendations of the AI4KGA based on the transcripts. The interview transcripts were then compared to identify responses that were identical. Regarding the quantitative methods, the data was processed using SPSS Version 20 and subjected to various analytical techniques, such as descriptive statistics, item analysis, reliability and validity assessments, ANOVA, and correlation analysis. In addition, STATA was used to estimate the parameters of discrimination and dif- ficulty using the 2PLM. R was used to test the information function and standard error of measurement. This allowed us to evaluate the psychometric properties of the AI4KGA, such as its reliability, validity, and item difficulty. The statistical analyses also provided insight into the effects of age and gender on the AI literacy scores of the kindergarten students. The results of the quantitative data analysis complemented the findings of the qualitative analysis, providing a comprehensive understanding of the AI literacy levels of kindergarten students and the efficacy of the AI4KGA in evaluating their AI literacy.

**4 Results**

**4.1 RQ1: Is the AI4KGA a valid and reliable measure of kindergarten children’s AI literacy?**

The validity of the AI4KGA was validated through two methods: expert validation and item analysis. Expert validation includes four parts: (1) face validity, (2) con- struct validity, (3) content validity, and (4) suggestions.

**4.1.1 Expert validation**

**Face Validity** Several criteria were used to evaluate the face validity of the AI4KGA These included: (1) determining the level of question difficulty appropriate for chil- dren aged 3–6 in kindergarten; (2) utilizing clear illustrations to explain the questions and options; and (3) ensuring that an appropriate number of questions were included. Regarding question difficulty, the majority experts felt that the difficulty level was ‘neither easy nor difficult’, with ‘somewhat difficult’ being the next most common response (Fig. 1). The majority of experts also indicated that the AI4KGA’s clear illustrations to explain questions and options were the most helpful aspects, with ‘neither clear nor unclear’ and ‘somewhat clear’ being the next most commonre- sponses (Fig. 2). The majority of experts also showed that the number of questions is suitable.

**Construct Validity** The experts were queried regarding the suitability of the AI4KG assessment that had been modified to evaluate the basic AI knowledge of kinder- garten children. The findings indicated that the majority of experts concurred that the AI4KGA was well suited for evaluating the AI literacy of kindergarten children, with neutral being the next most common response. These results suggest that the construct validity of the AI4KGA is appropriate.

**Content Validity** The experts were tasked with evaluating the content validity of the AI4KG assessment by determining whether the questions related to AI tools were a suitable representation of AI tool skills. The findings revealed that the majority of experts responded positively, indicating that the AI tools assessment was an ade- quate representation of AI tool skills. The experts were also asked to verify that the assessment was suitable for kindergarten children in the 3–6 age range. Most experts believed that it was suitable for children aged 3–6.

In addition to the survey responses, experts also provided further insights into their opinion on the validity of the AI4KGA content through open-ended comments and individual interviews. Regarding the content validity of the AI4KG assessment for kindergarten children, some experts were particularly concerned about two aspects: 

1. the appropriateness of language and images and (2) the appropriateness of knowl- edge points. These experts raised concerns about whether the language used in the

assessment was appropriate for kindergarten children’s understanding abilities, as well as whether the knowledge points in the assessment were suitable for their cogni- tive levels and developmental stages.

The research findings show that majority of experts indicated that the language and knowledge points in the assessment were both suitable for children aged 3–6, in terms of their cognitive levels and developmental stages. However, two experts noted that the last question of the AI literacy assessment may be somewhat challenging for 3-year-old children, while two other experts believed that the Teachable Machine tool questions may be difficult for 3-year-olds to comprehend.

**Suggestions** We improved the validity of the assessment by conducting individual interviews with teachers and researchers asking open-ended questions in a survey. Two kindergarten educators and one researcher suggested adding an “I don’t know” option so that children would not feel pressured to choose an answer. This addition also helps to distinguish between children who did not have enough time to answer the question and those who do not know the correct answer. A researcher from Hong Kong suggested adding observation methods. The assessment process should include various methods such as observation and questionnaires to obtain comprehensive and accurate assessment results for children.

**4.1.2 Verifying the unidimensionality assumption**

To validate the assumption of unidimensionality, we conducted a confirmatory fac- tor analysis (CFA) by fitting a one-factor model to the set of 16 items. The results of the CFA showed that the model fitted the data well (X2 (_98_) = 163.010; _p_ = .000; RMSEA = 0.056). Furthermore, all of the items loaded high and significantly on their corresponding latent factors.

**4.1.3 Item analysis**

First and foremost, the Cronbach’s _α_ coefficient was used to test the assessment’s reliability. Cronbach’s _α_ is a widely used measure of reliability that quantifies the degree of random measurement error present in a sum score or average calculated from a multi-item measurement assessment (Hayes & Coutts, [2020)](#declarations). The results of the reliability test presented in Table 4 indicate that all items are compositely reliable, with Cronbach’s _α_ values range between 0.757 and 0.790. All items are above the reliability standard 0.7 (\> 0.7). Therefore, the assessment demonstrated good reli- ability. Overall, this conclusion indicates that the AI4KGA developed in this study has demonstrated reliability and is suitable for measuring the AI literacy abilities of kindergarten children.

We then estimated the parameters of discrimination and difficulty using the 2PLM. The use of the Item Response Theory (IRT) has been suggested in the context of instrument validation (e.g., Toraman et al., 2022; Aesaert et al., [2014;](#declarations) Kong & Lai, 2022). In my study, we employed a two-parameter model that yielded information about both the difficulty level and discrimination ability of each question. The dis- crimination index of a question indicates its ability to distinguish between low and high performers, and it is ideal to have questions with varying levels of difficulty and high discrimination. Figure 3 (Item Characteristic Curves) and Fig. 4 (Item Infor- mation Curves) show the IRT results. The Item Characteristic Curve (ICC) is an S-shaped curve that shows the probability of electing the correct answer in AI4KGA at a given AI literacy ability level. The curve’s peak location indicates the difficulty level, with more challenging questions peaking towards the higher (right) end of the x-axis (ability). The steepness of the curve reflects the item’s discrimination, with steeper curves indicating better discrimination.

The Item Characteristic Curves (ICCs) exhibit peaks at different ability levels, indicating that AI4KG assessment effectively challenges children with both low and high AI literacy levels. The curves vary in steepness, while all questions demonstrate acceptable levels of discrimination. The mean discrimination index was 1.09, and the mean difficulty index for all questions was − 1.07. The difficulty parameter pertains to the level of difficulty associated with answering an item correctly, where a nega- tive value indicates that the item is relatively easy and a positive value suggests that

it is relatively challenging for someone with an average ability level (Al-zboon & Alrekebat, [2021)](#declarations).

Item Information Curves (IIC) show the amount of information about an item’s latent ability. The Item Information Curve (IIC) peak represents the point at which the item has the highest discrimination. In the current sample, we observe peaks occurring at the left, middle, or right end of the x-axis (latent ability), as shown in Fig. 4. This sample indicates that this assessment can provide information about kindergarten students’ abilities across different levels of AI proficiency, including high, medium, and low levels. Results show that Q6 provides the most information about high ability levels (the peak of its IIC is farthest to the right), and Q16 pro- vides the most information about lower ability levels (the peak of its IIC is farthest to the left).

In Fig. 5, we present the success rate per item, expressed as a per-unit value or the item difficulty index. The average success rate along the 16 items is _p_ = .57 (medium difficulty), ranging from _p_ = .368 (Q6; very high difficulty) to _p_ = .83 (Q1; very low difficulty).

Figure 6 displays the assessment information function and standard error of mea- surement. The summary in R software shows the assessment information was the highest and the standard error was the lowest at stability levels of approximately −0.33 to −0.38. Figure 7 shows the assessment’s reliability at the different ability levels. Specifically, at ability levels approximately between − 0.33 to -0.38, _r_ = .874. Furthermore, for ability levels around − 1.7 to 1.1, _r_ had a value more than 0.70, indi- cating that the assessment’s precision was satisfactory in this range.

**4.2 Age and gender differences**

We conducted a two-way ANOVA to assess the main and interaction effects of age and gender on the AI4KG assessment scores. Tables 5 and 6 present the correspond- ing means and standard deviations (SDs), and ANOVA results.

Due to the moderate sample size of the study, even minor differences could pro- duce significant results. Therefore, we calculated the effect sizes based on partial eta squared, as presented in Table 6. A value of 0.01 indicates a small effect, 0.06 a medium effect, and 0.14 a large effect (Cohen et al., 1988). As Table 6 shows,

the effects of age and gender were significant, and their interaction effect was also significant.

As shown in Table 6, the large effect size of 0.745 indicates that age had a signifi- cant effect. The results indicated that children who were six years old (13.33) had significantly higher AI literacy scores than those who were four (5.63) and five years old (8.56). These findings suggests that older children performed better than younger children in the AI4KG assessment. This result further supports the validity of the final version of the AI4KG assessment when combined with the objective expert evalua- tion of the criteria.

Table 6 shows that gender had a significant effect, with a medium effect size of 0.117. The results indicated that the girls (9.18) appeared to have a slightly higher ability level than the boys (9.14) in terms of AI literacy score after completing the curriculum.

**5 Discussion**

In recent years, there has been a growing body of research focused on integrat- ing AI literacy into early childhood education. To date, there have been no vali- dated and reliable tests to assess AI literacy in kindergarten children. To address this gap, we developed the AI4KG assessment (AI4KGA), a multiple-choice test. AI4KGA was specifically designed to be developmentally appropriate for chil- dren between the ages of 3 and 6 years. The main objective of this study was to measure and validate the AI4KGA. The resulting 16 items questions have been validated using an expert evaluation (i.e., face, construct, and content validity) and Cronbach’s _α_ approach using SPSS software. We estimated the parameters of discrimination and difficulty using the 2PLM in STATA. As a result, this study offers resources for educators and researchers to assess the learning outcomes of children and adjust the curriculum and pedagogical approaches accordingly.

**5.1 A valid and reliable measure of kindergarten children’s AI literacy**

Results on 215 kindergarten children showed that all the 16 assessment items had suf- ficient reliability as evidenced by Cronbach’s _α_ approach and face, construct, and content validity as per expert-based approach. The validated instrument can be used to assess the learning gains of children in terms of AI literacy in the context of ECE. IRT analysis shows that the difficulty level of the measurement tool is generally suitable for kinder- garten students. The results indicated that AI4KG assessment is a valid and reliable tool for measuring AI literacy in kindergarten children. We plan to use AI4KG assessment to assess more kindergarten students and lower primary school students in future research. This is the first developed AI literacy assessment for kindergarten children. Previous studies only focused on designing some questions to evaluate kindergarten children’s AI literacy without verifying their reliability (e.g., Williams et al., 2019b). For example, Williams (2019b) developed an AI literacy assessment for kindergarten children to assess their three AI concepts, namely knowledge-based system, supervised machine learning, and generative AI. However, this study did not mention the validated and reliable AI literacy assessment. Our study uses various methods to measure and validate the AI4KG assessment, such as experts’ evaluation (e.g., face, construct, and content validity), Cron- bach’s _α_ analysis, and Item Response Theory (IRT).

The method used in this study, namely validation test, differs from that of other studies. Some researchers developed a computational thinking assessment to assess the compu- tational thinking of secondary school students (Román-González et al., 2017). Román- González et al. (2017) used several approaches, such as correlation analysis and multiple linear regression, to validate the computational thinking assessment. Moreover, Tzafilkou et al. (2022) utilized confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) to validate a scale that measures students’ digital competence. Despite that using a validation assessment method different from other scholars, the results indicate that the assessment designed in this study is reli- able in terms of validity and reliability. This study could help educators and AI research- ers in assessing the learning outcomes of kindergarten children and can assist them in adjusting their curriculum methods.

**5.2 Age and gender differences in AI literacy scores**

We found that the AI literacy scores of the children tended to increase with age. This finding is consistent with other studies, which have concluded that students’ cognitive level generally improves with age (Cuellar,[ 2015)](#declarations). This study is also consistent with other studies of AI literacy in early childhood education, such as that of Williams et al. (2019a), who found that kindergarten children had higher scores than pre-K children. Although many factors can affect cognitive development, age is generally regarded as a significant predictor of cognitive ability, with performance tending to improve as children’s age. Girls were observed to have a slightly higher level of AI literacy than boys after com- pleting the AI literacy curriculum. Further studies are required to assess whether there is a gender difference in AI literacy in higher kindergarten grades (K3). Given the potentially large variations in children’s characteristics across regions, conducting further research on diverse student populations will strengthen and validate the findings.

**5.3 Implications for policy and practice**

The study has various important implications for policy and practice. The results of this research could potentially have impact on policy-makers. Government and relevant organizations can utilize the data collected using this new AI4KGA tool to shape related policies about incorporating AI literacy into kindergarten curriculum. For instance, this study’s findings showed that kindergarten children can grasp fundamental AI knowledge and concepts. Policy-makers can consider encouraging the incorporation of AI literacy courses into kindergarten curricula. In general, integrating AI literacy curriculum into early childhood education can foster children’s creativity and problem-solving skills. Educators and instructional designers in educational institutions also have a crucial role in promoting AI literacy among children. They can utilise the developed and vali- dated AI4KGA in this study to design appropriate curricula and syllabi for kindergarten children, which can be implemented through formal and informal training. This can help children develop the necessary knowledge and skills to understand and use AI technology effectively.

The findings of this study can guide educational institutions that plan to develop AI literacy courses for children. We developed and validated the AI4KG assessment can be used to evaluate the effectiveness of such courses and identify areas for improvement, helping to ensure that children receive high-quality AI literacy education. Finally, a validated AI literacy assessment tool can serve as a practical and useful tool to evaluate kindergarten children’s AI literacy, including their knowledge and skills on recent technological trends like AI and its applications in daily life, This tool can be used in kindergarten institutions and education centers to assess and improve children’s AI literacy, which is becoming increasingly important in the digital age.

**5.4 Limitations**

First, the relatively small sample size for validation was a limitation of this study. Although the sample size was adequate according to Cronbach’s _α_, the expert survey, the interview method, and IRT, further research is encouraged with larger populations. Second, we only examined differences in AI4KGA based on gender and age. However, future research could investigate other factors that may affect AI literacy assessment, such as family socio-economic status and geographical differences.

**6 Conclusion**

This study developed and validated an AI4KGA to measure AI literacy in kindergar- ten children. The AI4KG assessment provide a conceptual framework for understanding the main components of AI literacy in the context of early childhood education. Results showed that kindergarten children could understand basic AI knowledge in the AI4KG assessment.

The AI4KGA can be useful for assessing and improving AI literacy in kindergarten children. Additionally, researchers specialising in AI literacy can use it as a valuable resource when studying the effectiveness of different teaching approaches and pedagogi-

cal methods. The validity and reliability of the AI4KGA were assessed through expert- based, Cronbach’s α, and IRT approaches demonstrating high validity, consistency, and reliability. We found that younger children had lower scores on AI4KGA than older chil- dren. We also found that girls demonstrated a slightly higher AI literacy score than boys after they completed the AI4KG curriculum. The AI4KG assessment can be adapted to assess AI literacy in kindergarten students, which can help improve and encourage the AI literacy of young children in the digital age and advance research in this area.
